profile.reading:
This is Equinix's ML3 facility at Via Ennio Doris 13 in Basiglio, a comune in the greater Milan metropolitan area; this row carried no operator website URL on file until a same-day research pass located Equinix's dedicated ML3 page by matching the URL pattern already on file for sibling Italy and Finland rows. That page describes ML3 as a six-story, reinforced-concrete building, the tallest confirmed among the international facilities in this registry, with 2,102 square meters, about 22,626 square feet, of colocation space, N power redundancy (without the N+1 redundancy most sibling facilities publish), N+1 cooling redundancy, and a 99.9999%-plus global uptime guarantee; it does not publish a specific IT capacity figure in megawatts or kilowatts. Equinix entered the European colocation market through its 2007 acquisition of IXEurope and expanded further through its 2015 acquisition of TelecityGroup for about $3.8 billion, though Equinix's current ML3 page does not attribute the building to either predecessor company by name. Equinix, founded in Silicon Valley in 1998, converted to a real estate investment trust in January 2015 and trades on Nasdaq as EQIX.

As an EU-based facility, this data center falls under the European Union's Energy Efficiency Directive reporting requirements, which since 2024 have required data centers above a minimum capacity threshold to report power usage effectiveness, water usage, and other sustainability metrics to a European Commission database, part of a broader EU push for standardized data center energy transparency that does not have a direct equivalent in most of the US markets covered elsewhere in this registry.

Italy's data center market has grown substantially in recent years as international operators including Equinix have expanded beyond Milan's traditional financial-sector core into surrounding comuni like Settimo Milanese and Basiglio, where larger, more affordable parcels have supported bigger facilities than central Milan real estate typically allows, while Milan itself remains Italy's primary internet exchange and financial-services hub.
